Using air instead of biogas for mixing and its effect on anaerobic digestion of 
animal wastewater with high suspended solids 
Hongnan Yanga,b, Liangwei Denga,b,⁎ 
a Biogas Institute of Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Chengdu 610041, PR China 
b Laboratory of Development and Application of Rural Renewable Energy, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Chengdu 610041, PR China 
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Anaerobic digestion 
Animal wastewater 
Air mixing 
Microaeration 
A B S T R A C T   
This study proposed a new mixing method for anaerobic digestion treating animal wastewater using air as gas 
source of agitation (named “air mixing”) and demonstrated its feasibility by comparing with other mixing 
modes. The results indicated that the methane production for air mixing was increased by 6.4%, 11.9% and 
19.6% compared with biogas mixing, mechanical mixing and no mixing. Air mixing improved the mass transfer 
and the homogeneous mixing time was shortened from 10 min of mechanical mixing to 1.5 min at the same 
power input. A transient microaerobic environment was created by air mixing, which increased the hydrolysis 
efficiency by 1.7–11.4% compared with biogas mixing and facilitated VFAs generation and consumption, as well 
as promoted the syntrophic relationship between facultative bacteria and hydrogenotrophic methanogens. The 
relative contribution of the improvement of mass transfer and the reaction of microaerobic environment to 
methane production was 62.9% and 37.1%, respectively.   
1. Introduction 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is an effective method for the treatment of 
animal wastewater (Yang et al., 2019). However, the presence of high 
suspended solids (> 2000 mg L−1) in the wastewater causes the diffi­
culty of mass transfer in the system and the formation of scum and 
sediment, and negatively impacts functioning and performance of 
anaerobic reactors (Zeng et al., 2019). Proper mixing during anaerobic 
treatment is considered to be an effective method to increase biomass 
conversion efficiency and methane yield because mixing distributes 
substrates, enzymes, microorganisms and temperature throughout the 
digester. The importance of mixing has been reported by many re­
searchers (Kariyama et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2019). From a detailed 
review of the digestion process and commercial large-scale digesters, 
the mixing of an anaerobic digester is accomplished through a motor- 
driven mixer (i.e., mechanical mixing), recirculation of the mixed

liquor (i.e., hydraulic mixing) or biogas (i.e., biogas mixing) (Kariyama 
et al., 2018). 
Advantages and disadvantages of various mixing methods in anae­
robic digesters are well documented in the literature (Latha et al., 2019; 
Singh et al., 2019). Mechanical mixing has been proved to be more 
economical than recirculation in terms of power consumption per vo­
lume mixed (Singh et al., 2019); however, the mechanical parts inside 
the digester are not easily accessible for maintenance (Latha et al., 
2019). Hydraulic mixing is more flexible and less prone to gas leakage 
than mechanical mixing, but has difficulty mixing the substrate and 
sludge thoroughly. “Short circuits” and “dead spaces” where hydraulic 
mixing is inadequate are common in digesters (Bhattacharjee et al., 
2015). Therefore, hydraulic mixing is generally only suitable for small 
reactors that treat wastewaters having low solids concentrations (Karim 
et al., 2005). Biogas mixing achieves good mass transfer and heat 
transfer at low energy consumption and uses a simple configuration 
that has no moving parts inside the digester. It is generally recognized 
that biogas mixing is superior to other modes of mixing in terms of 
energy requirement, operation costs and reliability over long-term op­
eration (Kuczman et al., 2017; Latha et al., 2019). However, biogas 
mixing is not frequently used in on-farm biogas plants because it creates 
difficulty in maintaining sufficient mixing when the biogas production 
is low. In addition, relatively expensive explosion-proof motors and 
other safety devices are needed when pumping biogas for mixing. 
It is reasonable to question whether air instead of biogas is used for 
mixing the contents of anaerobic digesters, thereby resolving the pro­
blems of insufficient biogas production and safety. So far, no research 
has been reported about using ambient air as the gas source for mixing 
in AD. In fact, exposing AD systems to oxygen (or air) traditionally has 
been avoided because of its negative effects on the growth and activity 
of obligate anaerobes, especially methanogens, by damaging the cell 
membrane, crucial proteins, and other cell constituents (Bhattad et al., 
2017). However, it has been found in recent years that strict anaerobes 
have several mechanisms that allow them to tolerate oxygen or air and 
experience few or no inhibitory effects (Botheju and Bakke, 2011; 
Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). Numerous researchers have applied mi­
croaeration in the AD process, which is achieved by injecting a limited 
amount of air or oxygen into the digester to enhance hydrolysis, control 
accumulation of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and remove hydrogen sul­
fide (H2S) (Krayzelova et al., 2015; Nguyen and Khanal, 2018; Nguyen 
et al., 2019; Ruan et al., 2019). However, these studies injected air/ 
oxygen into the headspace of digesters or into the liquid mixture at a 
low gas flow rate in the range 3–10 mL/L/min (Nguyen and Khanal, 
2018). In other words, the purposes of air/oxygen injection into the 
digesters in previous studies were not for mixing, but rather for pro­
ducing a microaerobic environment. 
In this research, the novel idea of using air instead of biogas as a gas 
source for gas mixing (named “air mixing”) was studied with the ob­
jective of establishing a new mixing technology. To achieve this ob­
jective, several scientific questions had to be answered. First, can air 
mixing achieve adequate agitation without causing a substantial ne­
gative impact on the anaerobic environment for methane production? 
Second, what is the longest continuous air injection time that can be 
employed without affecting the anaerobic environment for methane 
production? Third, if air mixing is feasible and increases the efficiency 
of anaerobic digestion, what are the relative contributions of mixing 
and a microaerobic environment? 
Therefore, the overall goal of this study was to assess the feasibility 
of air mixing and evaluate its effects on the AD process based on the 
methane production efficiency. By combining reactor performance and 
microbial community analyses, new insights were sought into the re­
sponse of AD to air mixing so that an effective new mixing strategy for 
increasing the methane production of an AD system could be devel­
oped. 
2. Material and methods 
2.1. Reactor 
Four, 4.5 L anaerobic sequencing batch reactors, each with a 
working volume of 4.0 L (11 cm internal diameter, 45 cm liquid 
height), were used (Fig. 1). Reactors 1 (R-a) and Reactors 2 (R-b) were 
mixed by air and biogas, respectively. The gas was introduced into the 
reactors via a digital peristaltic pump and an aeration disc at the bottom 
of the reactors. Reactor 3 (R-m) was mixed using a 6-cm diameter axial- 
flow impeller (NZ-1300, Eyela, Tokyo, Japan). Reactor 4 (R-n) was 
operated as blank control without any mixing. Each reactor was 
equipped with three sampling ports at different heights along the side of 
the reactor, as shown in Fig. 1.

2.2. Substrate and inoculum 
Swine wastewater was used as the substrate and was collected from 
a farm located in Jianyang, Sichuan, China. Samples were transported 
back to the laboratory immediately after collection and stored at 4 °C 
prior to use. The swine wastewater was diluted with a certain amount of 
tap water to achieve a total solids (TS) concentration of 6%. The in­
oculation sludge for the AD experiments was harvested from a labora­
tory-scale mesophilic anaerobic digester that treated swine wastewater 
(Supporting Information). 
2.3. Comparison experiments of air mixing with other mixing modes 
To begin the experiments, 2 L of inoculum sludge was added to each 
reactor. The four reactors were fed swine wastewater once per day 
(semi-continuous mode) at a loading rate of 6.0 g VS/L/d. The steady 
state was defined to be the point when biogas production varied within 
10% of the mean between feeding times within 2–3 weeks. Each reactor 
was maintained at 35  ±  1.0 °C by an electrically heated water jacket 
surrounding the reactor. Biogas was collected in aluminum gas-bags for 
subsequent analysis. 
The three reactors with mixing (R-a, R-b and R-m) were agitated 
three times per day for 1.5 min on each occasion: once immediately 
after feeding, once 2 h after feeding, and once 6 h after feeding. All 
three reactors were mixed at the same power input per unit volume of 
mixed liquid condition (i.e., 5 W/m3). The gas flow rate for R-a and R-b 
and the impeller speed for R-m were calculated as described by Karim 
et al. (2005). Detailed calculation is given in supporting information. A 
gas flow rate of 66.7 mL/L/min was supplied to reactors R-a and R-b 
and the R-m was operated at 88 rpm. 
2.4. Degree of mixing 
The degree of mixing of the digester contents was reflected by the 
TS distribution within the reactors, which was determined by collecting 
samples for TS analysis from three different heights (10, 20 and 30 cm) 
above the base of the digesters after mixing. The coefficient of variance 
(κ) was defined by the ratio of standard variation of TS concentrations 
to average of TS concentrations as described in Eq. (1) and was used as 
a measure of degree of mixing. Furthermore, “homogeneous mixing 
time” was defined as the time required achieving a certain degree of 
mixing. In this paper, a κ-value less than 0.02, was considered to in­
dicate homogeneous mixing.

2.5. Analytical methods 
The pH, ORP, and methane yield were monitored daily; individual 
VFA and biogas composition were analysed weekly; the crude protein, 
crude fiber and crude fat contents were determined monthly. Details of 
the analytical methods are provided in the Supporting Information. 
Comparisons among values obtained in four reactors were made by 
one-way repeated analysis of variance, followed by Dunnett’s t test. A 
value of p  <  0.05 was considered statistically significant. 
2.6. Microbiological analysis 
To assess the microbial community and population shift responding 
to mixing, sludge samples were collected from each reactor at the 
conclusion of the experiment. Total genomic DNA was extracted using a 
PowerSoil DNA Isolation Kit (MO BIO, Carlsbad, CA, USA) according to 
the manufacturer’s protocol. The primer pairs 344F-915R and 338F- 
806R were used to amplify the archaeal 16S rRNA genes and bacterial 
16S rRNA genes as described in Yang et al. (2019). Detailed method 
description can be found in the Supporting Information. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Reactor performance in different mixing modes 
3.1.1. Volumetric methane production rate 
The volumetric methane production rate is defined as the methane 
production per volume of digester per day and is a good indicator of the 
digester efficiency. Mean values for the volumetric methane production 
rate in the four reactors were determined based on steady-state con­
ditions and are summarized in Table 1. The volumetric methane pro­
duction rates of R-a, R-b, R-m and R-n were 1.371, 1.288, 1.225 and 
1.146 L/L/d, respectively. The total methane production was sig­
nificantly greater for three reactors with mixing than the reactor 
without mixing, which implied that a short mixing time of only 1.5 min 
enhanced the AD process. Kaparaju et al.(2008) had a similar finding; 
they observed that compared with biogas production from continuous 
mechanical mixing, production from minimal mixing (10 min mixing 
before feeding) increased by 12.5%. Among the four reactors, the dif­
ferences in total methane production were statistically significant (one- 
way ANOVA, p  <  0.05). The total methane production for R-a was the 
highest and increased by 6.4%, 11.9% and 19.6% compared with R-b, 
R-m and R-n, respectively. It was evident that air mixing not only did 
not limit methanogenesis, but also promoted the production of me­
thane. 
The biogas production rates (mL/min) during the 24 h after feeding 
are shown in Fig. 2. In the three reactors with mixing systems, the 
biogas production rate remained high in the first 12 h, in contrast to 
that in the reactor without mixing. Furthermore, a significant increase 
in the rate of biogas production per min was observed after each of the 
three mixing periods because mixing promoted the mass transfer and 
the release of CH4. The digesters were not mixed in the subsequent 
12 h, and there was no difference in the biogas production rates among 
digesters R-b, R-m and R-n, but the biogas production rate of R-a was 
obviously greater than other three reactors. ORP profiles of the R-a

biogas production rate in R-a may have occurred because some re­

3.1.2. Methane yield 
Methane yield is the volume of methane produced per unit mass of 
VS added, and is an effective parameter by which to judge methane 
production efficiency in terms of loaded substrate. Previously, re­
searchers reported that the injection of air into anaerobic digesters 
could result in some organic matter being consumed by the aerobic 
oxidation, thereby decreasing the methane yield (Díaz et al., 2010). 
Methane yields during the stable stage of AD are shown in Table 1 and 
were observed to be 0.229, 0.215, 0.205 and 0.191 LCH4/gVSadded, for 
R-a, R-b, R-m and R-n, respectively, at VS solid loading of 6 g L−1 d−1. 
The methane yield of R-n is similar to the results from AD experiments 
using swine manure as the substrate gave specific methane productions 
not exceeding 0.2 LCH4/gVSadded (Borowski et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2019) 
when the loading rate exceeded 4 g VS L−1 d−1. In this study, the 
mixing increased methane yield by 7.3%–19.9%. Compared to the 
methane yield of R-b and R-m, the methane yield of R-a increased by as 
much as 6.5% and 11.7%, respectively. These increases indicated that 
instead of decreasing methane yield, the transient microaerobic en­
vironment created by air-mixing in R-a actually improved the conver­
sion of organic matter to CH4 compared to that from the digesters that 
had other types of mixing. 
3.1.3. Biogas composition 
The mean values for biogas composition were determined based on 
steady-state conditions and are summarized in Table 1. The average 
CH4 content in the biogas produced in R-b and R-m were not sig­
nificantly different from that in biogas from R-n and ranged from 60.2% 
to 60.9%. By contrast, the average CH4 content in biogas from R-a 
(53.8%) were lower by 10.6–11.6%. The CH4 content in the outlet of 
the R-a declined to 33% after air mixing for 1.5 min as a result of the 
dilution by air used for mixing as shown in Fig. 3, and subsequently 
gradually increased and returned to its initial value of over 54% in 
1.5 h. The injection air leaving the digester with the biogas into the gas- 
bags represented a content of 10–12% in biogas composition as shown 
in Table 1. The CH4/CO2 ratio of biogas from R-a was 1.59, which was 
slightly lower than that in biogas from the other reactors (1.70–1.77) 
(Table 1). These results suggests that the aerobic oxidation of the 
organic matter to produce CO2 was also a reason of the decrease in the 
CH4 content observed in R-a. 
The H2S contents in R-a, R-b, R-m and R-n were 100, 271, 293 and 
336 ppm, respectively (Table 1), and thus, the efficiency of desulfur­
ization achieved by air mixing was 70.2%. This was significantly higher 
than the desulfurization efficiencies achieved by biogas mixing (19.3%) 
and mechanical mixing (12.8%), but not as high as reported (98–99%) 
in a previous study (Nghiem et al., 2014; Krayzelova et al., 2015). The 
almost complete desulfurization reported probably occurred because 
the technique used was like that of most microaerobic reactor methods, 
i.e., injecting air or O2 directly into the headspace of the reactor where 
H2S oxidation mainly takes place (Díaz et al., 2011; Krayzelova et al., 
2015). By contrast, in the present study, air was injected directly into 
the liquid phase where the O2 could have been consumed by other 
oxidative processes in addition to the oxidation of H2S. In fact, the H2S 
removal efficiency obtained in this study was similar to that reported by  
Krayzelova et al. (2014) of 73% who injected air into the liquid phase of 
an anaerobic digester. Although the efficiency of H2S removal with air 
mixing was lower than the efficiency when air was applied in the 
headspace, but the decrease in the sulfide concentration in the liquid 
had an additional positive effect of decreasing the effect of sulfide 
toxicity on methanogens (Krayzelova et al., 2015). Fig. 3(C) shows the 
evolution of H2S in biogas before and after mixing. The H2S levels de­
creased after air injection (R-a) and then gradually increased, which

3.2. Mechanistic analysis of the positive effects of air mixing on AD 
3.2.1. Improved mass transfer by mixing 
As described in Section 2.3, the coefficient of variation (κ) of the TS 
concentrations at different depths in the digesters was used as a 
quantitative measure of the degree of mixing. A κ-value less than 0.02 
(as calculated using Eq. (1)) indicated homogeneous mixing. Only the 
axial variation of TS concentrations was used to compare mixing per­
formance because the high height-to-diameter ratio (4.2) of the diges­
ters meant that axial mixing was a more time-consuming process than 
latitudinal mixing. Fig. 4 shows the variation of κ-values for different 
mixing techniques as a function of mixing time. At time (t) = 0 min, 
namely no mixing, TS was naturally distributed by gravity and many 
solids settled in the lower layer of the reactors. The κ-values for the 
different reactors were at their maxima (0.145–0.165) at this time. As 
mixing time increased, the substrate and sludge in the reactors were 
mixed and eventually TS became evenly distributed throughout the 
whole reactor. The κ-value in R-a decreased greatly with the increase of 
mixing time from 0 to 1.5 min and then approached a stable value of 
0.016. The change of κ-values in R-b was not much different from that 
in R-a, which indicated that the homogeneous mixing time of both gas- 
mixed reactors were less than 1.5 min. However, the amplitude of the 
variation of κ-values in R-m was smaller than that for the two gas-mixed 
reactors and the time needed to reach a stable κ-value was about 
10 min, which indicated that mechanical mixing required much longer 
to achieve homogenization than gas mixing. Mao et al. (2019) also 
reported a long time of 19 min required for an impeller-mixed digester 
to reach homogeneous mixing under similar a mixing condition. 
The stable value of κ was about 0.025 in R-m and higher than the 
stable values in R-a and R-b (0.016 and 0.017, respectively), which may 
be due to the flow fields generated by the different mixing modes. In 
both gas-mixed reactors, bubbles released from the bottom of reactors 
mixed the digester contents by physically moving the substrate and 
sludge as the bubbles rose to the surface. The small gas bubbles also 
lowered the density and viscosity of the bulk solution; consequently, 
the digester contents in the gas-mixed reactors were easier to move and 
mix than those in the mechanically mixed reactor (Low, 2014). Pre­
vious research on radial-flow impellers for mechanical mixing showed 
that radial mixing was not totally effective for solid suspensions 
(Leonzio, 2019); although radial mixing was good, axial mixing was 
less so. Therefore, the results from the current study indicated that 
compared with no mixing, all three mixing modes improved the mass 
transfer effect. Moreover, both gas-mixed reactors achieved a higher 
mixing efficiency and better homogeneous mixing within a shorter 
mixing time than the mechanically mixed reactor. 
3.2.2. Facilitated hydrolysis and VFA generation and consumption 
AD is accomplished by microorganisms in different trophic groups, 
including hydrolysis, acidogenesis, syntrophic acetogenesis, and me­
thanogenesis groups (Batstone et al., 2002). The initial hydrolysis of 
particulate complex substrates to soluble forms is a rate-limiting step 
during AD of complex organic matter such as animal wastewater. 
Proteins, carbohydrates, fiber and fat are major particulate components 
of swine wastewater and account for more than 50% of the TS. 
Therefore, changes of these particulate constituents in the solid phase 
can be used to describe hydrolysis efficiency. Hydrolyses of the protein, 
carbohydrates, fiber and fat under different digester mixing modes were 
shown in Table 2. As expected, mixing significantly increased the hy­
drolysis efficiencies with which these substances were degraded 
(1.6–34.7%) in comparison to the reactor without mixing (R-n) 
(p  <  0.05). A uniform distribution of substrates, enzymes and micro- 
organisms throughout the digesters during mixing played an important 
role in achieving the improved efficiencies. There was significant dif­
ference in hydrolysis efficiency of the protein, carbohydrates, fiber and 
fat between R-a and other three reactors (Dunnett’s t test). The highest 
protein, fiber and carbohydrates removal efficiencies were obtained in 
R-a, for which hydrolysis efficiencies were 1.7–11.4%, 7.7–23.8% and 
21.0–29.1% higher than those in R-b, R-m and R-n, respectively. The fat 
removal efficiency in R-a was second only to that in R-b. These results 
indicated that air mixing promoted the hydrolysis efficiency of parti­
culate complex substrates. On the one hand, mixing promoted a uni­
form distribution of substrate and microorganisms (Singh et al., 2019). 
On the one hand, it was likely that injected oxygen could support the 
growth of and metabolism of facultative bacteria, leading to more hy­
drolytic enzyme production and improved the hydrolysis efficiency (Fu 
et al., 2016; Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). As shown by Fu et al. (2016), a 
daily oxygen supply obviously improved the hydrolysis rate of corn 
straw and some recalcitrant organic matter was also degraded. 
VFAs are produced by fermentation of hydrolysis products and are 
used in CH4 production. Fig. 5 illustrates the variation of VFAs con­
centrations (acetate, propionate and total VFA (TVFA)) in four reactors 
during the 24 h after feeding. Acetate concentration tended to fluctuate 
throughout the period, but the standard deviation of concentrations 
was less than 10%, which suggested that the production and con­
sumption of acetate might have occurred simultaneously. Nevertheless, 
the VFA concentrations in the four reactors differed. The TVFA

in an obstruction of VFA degradation by symbiotic microflora. The 
TVFA concentration in R-a ranged from 300 mg/L to 620 mg/L and was 
higher than that in R-b (300–550 mg/L) and R-m (250–450 mg/L). The 
greater VFAs production in R-a could be attributed to a transient mi­
croaerobic environment after air mixing, when the ORP increased to 
−250 mV. Alkaya and Demirer (2011) and Yin et al. (2016) showed 
that ORP values ranging between −100 mV and −300 mV enhanced 
the production of VFAs. Thus, in the present study air mixing increased 
the ORP to −250 mV and variations in the ORP might have promoted 
the formation of VFAs, thereby helping to improve the methane yield 
due to the production of more VFAs. 
3.2.3. Optimized syntrophic relationship among the microbial communities 
Bacterial and archaeal community structures at the genus level in 
samples from the four digesters are shown in Fig. 6. The most numerous 
genus Ruminofilibacter accounted for 19.2% of all bacteria in R-n, which 
was significantly higher than the abundance in three mixed reactors 
(6.8–11.8%) (Fig. 6 (A)). In comparison, Treponema_2 (instead of Ru­
minofilibacter) was the most dominant cellulose-degrading bacteria in 
the two gas mixed digesters (Huber and Stetter, 2015). Genus Clos­

Genera Acinetobacter and Rhodococcus were the main H2S-oxidizing

Archaeal communities demonstrated a clear dominance of the genus 
Methanosaeta, which represented 86.0–92.5% of all sequences identi­
fied in the four digesters (Fig. 4 (B)). The genus Methanospirillum was 
the second most abundant genus and comprised 7.6% of the archaeal 
population in R-a, but its abundance reduced by half in other three 
reactors. In AD systems, Methanosaeta are known to use acetate as the 
substrate for methanogenesis (via the acetotrophic pathway), whereas 
Methanospirillum use the CO2 reduction pathway with either H2/CO2 or 
formate as substrate (via the hydrogenotrophic pathway). An increase 
in the abundance of hydrogenotrophic methanogens such as Methano­
culleus also was reported in several studies about microaerobic systems 
(Tang et al., 2004; Ramos and Fdz-Polanco, 2013). There was a good 
balance of acetotrophic methanogenesis and hydrogenotrophic metha­
nogenesis in R-a and may be a reason for the high methane production 
compared to that in the other three reactors. In addition, the high re­
lative abundance of Methanospirillum in R-a indicated that more me­
thane could be produced via the interspecies H2/formate transfer 
pathway. This pathway may be considered as a remedy for decreased 
methane content in biogas due to an increase of CO2 caused by aerobic 
oxidation. 
3.2.4. Relative contributions of the improved mass transfer and the 
microaerobic environment to increased methane production 
The results presented thus far show that air mixing not only had no 
negative effect on AD, but also promoted the hydrolysis of particulate 
matter, allowing better solubilization for further anaerobic processes 
and improved methane production efficiency. Two main factors 
contributed to this increased efficiency. One was the improved mass 
transfer between the substrate and microorganisms due to mixing. The 
other was the transient microaerobic environment generated by the 
injection of air, which enabled both anaerobic and aerobic biological 
activities to occur within a single bioreactor. The relative contributions 
of the factors were analyzed based on data in Table 1. The results are 
presented in Table 3. 
The volumetric methane production rates for R-a, R-b and R-n were 
1.371, 1.288, 1.225 and 1.147 L/L/d, respectively (Table 1). The in­
crease of 0.224 L/L/d in R-a (compared with the rate in R-n) was re­
garded as the total contribution of the improved mass transfer com­
bined with the microaerobic environment. The increase of 0.083 L/L/d 
in R-a (compared with the rate in R-b) was regarded as the contribution 
of microaerobic environment. On this basis improved mass transfer was 
responsible for 62.9% of the improved methane production in R-a and 
the microaerobic environment was responsible for 37.1% of the im­
proved production. Similarly, the improved mass transfer was esti­
mated to be responsible for 48.9–93.5% of the hydrolysis efficiency of 
proteins, carbohydrates, fiber and fat. These results demonstrated that 
air mixing promoted methane production and hydrolysis more mainly 
by improving mass transfer than by generating a microaerobic en­
vironment. 
3.3. Significance and prospect of applying air mixing in practice 
The results of this study justify the conclusion that air mixing can be 
used as an alternative mixing method for AD and will enhance methane 
production. This is a new agitating approach for AD and achieves 
multiple functions, such as effective mixing, a creation of a micro­
aerobic environment, the improved efficiency of hydrolyzing solid or­
ganic matter and biological desulfurization, consequently improving 
methane production efficiency. 
Although air mixing may have a certain negative effect on the 
biogas composition due to dilution, the air content in the biogas in this 
study was approximately 10–12%, which was only slightly higher than 
that found by Tang et al. (2004) for the biogas that was desulfurized in 
the tank (2–7.5%). Less frequent mixing could further reduce the air 
content of the biogas. When a large amount of air is used for mixing, a 
three-way valve and solenoid valve can be set on the biogas outlet pipe. 
After air mixing, the gas discharged from the anaerobic digester can be 
discharged to the flare for combustion. The air content in the biogas can 
be completely controlled at a level as low as that in biogas desulfur­
ization in digester. Therefore, air mixing can be fully realized in prac­
tical engineering applications of AD. Because air mixing has many ad­
vantages, it is expected that this technology has promising application 
prospects. 
4. Conclusion 
This study proposed a new mixing method for anaerobic digestion 
treating animal wastewater using air as gas source of agitation (named 
“air mixing”) and demonstrated its feasibility by comparing with other 
mixing strategies. Air mixing showed great advantages in hydrolysis, 
methane production and the removal of hydrogen sulfide in biogas. The
